About this simulation

On screen
Left: the disc in perspective with σ = 1.0 μC/m², the z-axis, the point P at height z, a dashed radius a, and during Build the current ring of radius s′ and width ds′ with the line from P to it and the angle θ at P. The arrow at P is the running total of Ez on one fixed scale. Horizontal and vertical distances share one scale, so θ is drawn at its true size. Right: Ez against z, one colour per disc radius.
Controls
Disc radius a: 3, 10 or 30 cm, or an infinite plane; changing it removes the arrow until Build. Height z of P: 0.5 to 30 cm, locked during a sweep; after a build, moving it updates the field and traces the graph. Build sweeps the ring outwards in 6 s, steady in θ. Clear empties the graph.
Measured
Every field from the on-axis disc field of a uniform σ: the running total is the field of the disc out to the current ring. Ez in N/C, s′ and z in cm, θ in degrees, Q = πa²σ in nC.

Guided Inquiry

1 · Build the disc ring by ring

Keep the radius at 10 cm and the height at 5 cm. Before pressing Build, predict how the rings add up to the field at P as the ring sweeps out from the centre to the rim. Then press Build and watch the running total as the ring passes s′ = 5 cm.

2 · An infinite plane

Set the radius to the infinite plane, keep the height at 5 cm and press Build, and read the final field at P. Before moving P, predict the field when P is raised to 10 cm. Then move the height to 10 cm.

3 · Same angle, same share

Keep the infinite plane and the height of 10 cm. At a height of 5 cm the running total reached 1.65 × 104 N/C as the ring passed s′ = 5 cm, where the line from P makes 45° with the axis. Before pressing Build, predict at what ring radius the running total reaches the same value at the new height. Then press Build and watch the readouts.

4 · From plane-like to point-like

Set the radius to 10 cm and the height to 0.5 cm, press Clear and press Build. Before moving P, predict how Ez changes as P is raised slowly to 30 cm. Then raise it and watch the graph.

5 · Far away: a point charge

Set the radius to 3 cm and the height to 15 cm, press Build and read the field, about 1.10 × 103 N/C. Before moving P, predict the field when P is raised to 30 cm. Then move the height to 30 cm and read the field.

6 · Summary: a plane close up, a point far away

The field on the axis is the sum of the ring fields: Ez = (σ/2ε0)(1 − z/√(z² + a²)). The rings within an angle θ of the axis give the share (1 − cos θ) of the plane's field σ/2ε0, whatever the height.

Close to the disc, z much smaller than a, the rim is seen at nearly 90° and the field is almost the constant σ/2ε0 of an infinite plane. Far away, z much larger than a, the disc is seen within a small angle and the field is that of a point charge Q = πa²σ, falling as 1/z².

✦Learn this with the AI tutor

01

At a glance

This sim builds the electric field on the axis of a uniformly charged disc, ring by ring. Build sweeps a ring from the centre to the rim in 6 s, and an arrow at the point P above the disc shows the running total of Ez. A graph records Ez against the height z of P.

What you'll learn

  • How the field at P is the sum of the fields of thin rings.
  • How that field depends on the disc radius a and the height z.
  • What the field becomes when the disc is very large, or P is very far away.
The sim mid-sweep, sketched: a ring of radius s′ and width ds′ on a disc of radius a, the height z of P, and the angle θ at P. The arrow at P is the running Ez.

What's on screen

  • The disc, with charge density σ = 1.0 μC/m² and a dashed radius a. During Build the current ring, the line from P to it and the angle θ appear.
  • The arrow at P is the running total of Ez, on one fixed scale for every disc. A small plot above the disc follows the same total against θ.
  • The graph of Ez against z. Each disc radius has its own colour, and a finished build adds a point.
  • Readouts: the disc charge Q, the height z of P, the ring radius s′, the angle θ at P and the running Ez.
See itLook at the opening state, before any ring has been swept. Watch for: Disc charge Q reading 31.42 nC and Height z of P reading 5.0 cm, with the ring-sweep readouts still empty.

03

Each ring adds a field that peaks at s′ = z/√2

Slice the disc into thin rings (notes 1.2, Figure 6). A ring of radius s′ and width ds′ has area 2πs′ ds′ and charge

Every part of a ring is the same distance from P, so the field of a ring on its axis gives the ring's contribution to Ez (notes 1.17):

σ is the surface charge density and z the height of P.

A wider ring holds more charge, but it lies farther from P and its field is tilted away from the axis, so only the axial part survives. The two effects balance at s′ = z/√2, which is 3.54 cm for z = 5 cm.

The contribution per centimetre of ring radius for the opening disc, z = 5 cm. The shaded rings, out to s′ = 5 cm, give 53 % of the final field.

For a = 10 cm and z = 5 cm, the rings out to s′ = 5 cm hold a quarter of the charge, yet give 1.65 × 10⁴ N/C of the final 3.12 × 10⁴ N/C. The rings inside s′ = 1 cm give only 1.10 × 10³ N/C, 3.5 %.

Key idea. A ring's share of the field depends on its charge, its distance and its tilt together, not on its charge alone.
See itSweep the 10 cm disc, with P at 5 cm, until the ring reaches s′ = 5 cm. Watch for: Ring radius s′ reading 5.00 cm, Angle θ reading 45.00°, and Running Ez reading 1.65 × 10⁴ N/C.
04

Adding all the rings gives Ez = (σ/2ε₀)(1 − z/√(a² + z²))

Adding the rings from s′ = 0 to the rim s′ = a gives the field of the whole disc on its axis (notes 1.18 and 1.19):

The field points away from the disc for σ > 0. The sim shows z > 0 only.

For a = 10 cm and z = 5 cm the bracket is 1 − 5/√125 = 0.553, so Ez = 3.12 × 10⁴ N/C. The sweep ends at the rim, where θ = arctan(a/z) = 63.43°. The disc carries Q = πa²σ = 31.42 nC.

The bracket depends on a and z only through z/a. The 30 cm disc with P at 15 cm reads the same 3.12 × 10⁴ N/C.

disc a height z

These controls move the sim's too. Changing the radius removes the arrow, and z is locked during a sweep.

Go deeper: the integral

With w = s′² + z², so that dw = 2s′ ds′, the integral of s′ ds′/(s′² + z²)3/2 from 0 to a becomes ½∫w−3/2 dw taken from z² to a² + z². That equals 1/z − 1/√(a² + z²) (notes 1.18). Multiplying by σz/2ε₀ gives the bracket above.

See itLet the sweep finish on the 10 cm disc, with P at 5 cm. Watch for: Ring radius s′ at the rim, 10.00 cm, Angle θ at 63.43°, and Ez ending at 3.12 × 10⁴ N/C.
05

The rings within angle θ give the share 1 − cos θ of σ/2ε₀

Look from P. The line to a ring of radius s′ makes an angle θ with the axis, where cos θ = z/√(s′² + z²). Putting that into the sum gives the running total at that ring:

The sim's sweep is steady in θ, so θ rises at a constant rate and Ez follows this curve.
The running total against θ. The 10 cm disc at z = 5 cm stops at its rim angle, 63.4°.

The share depends on θ alone, not on z or a. A disc is a sweep that stops at its rim angle: 1 − cos 63.43° = 0.553 for the opening disc. A larger disc, or a lower P, stops at a larger angle, up to 90°.

Key idea. The share of the field from the rings within an angle θ of the axis depends on θ alone.
See itSweep the 10 cm disc, with P at 5 cm, until θ reaches 60°. Watch for: Angle θ reading 60.00°, Ring radius s′ reading 8.66 cm, and Running Ez reading 2.82 × 10⁴ N/C, half of σ/2ε₀.
06

An infinite plane has the same field E = σ/2ε₀ at every height

Let a grow without limit, or bring P close to the disc (z ≪ a). The second term in the bracket vanishes and the sweep reaches θ = 90° (notes 1.21):

With σ = 1.0 μC/m² this is 5.65 × 104 N/C. It does not depend on z.

Raising P weakens every ring, but the rings within any given angle of the axis then cover more of the plane. The two changes cancel exactly, so z does not appear in 1 − cos θ.

The same 45° at two heights above a plane. The ring is at s′ = z, so 5 cm for the lower P and 10 cm for the higher. The rings inside give 0.293 σ/2ε₀ = 1.65 × 104 N/C at both heights.

At z = 5 cm the running total passes 1.65 × 10⁴ N/C at s′ = 5 cm. At z = 10 cm it passes the same value at s′ = 10 cm, where the line from P again makes 45° with the axis.

Key idea. For a plane, the sweep always runs to 90°, so the final field is the same at every height.
Go deeper: below the plane

The disc looks the same from below, so the field there has the same magnitude and points the other way (notes 1.2). Across the plane the component along a fixed normal jumps by σ/ε₀ = 1.13 × 10⁵ N/C. The sim shows only z > 0.

See itFinish the sweep on the infinite plane with P at 5 cm, then raise P to 10 cm. Watch for: Height z of P changing from 5.0 to 10.0 cm while Running Ez stays at 5.65 × 10⁴ N/C.
See itNow sweep the plane, with P at 10 cm, until θ reaches 45°. Watch for: Ring radius s′ reading 10.00 cm, Angle θ reading 45.00°, and Running Ez reading 1.65 × 10⁴ N/C, as at 5 cm.
07

Close to the disc Ez stays near σ/2ε₀, then falls with z

For z ≪ a, P sees the rim at nearly 90°, and the disc behaves like the plane. The 10 cm disc gives 5.37 × 10⁴ N/C at z = 0.5 cm, 95 % of the plane value.

As z grows, the rim angle shrinks and Ez falls. For a = 10 cm it is half of σ/2ε₀ at z = a/√3 = 5.77 cm, where the rim is at 60°, then 1.65 × 10⁴ N/C at 10 cm and 2.90 × 10³ N/C at 30 cm. A larger disc stays near the plane value to greater heights.

Ez against z for the three discs. The dots mark the 10 cm disc at z = 0.5, 5.77, 10 and 30 cm. The dashed line is the plane value.

Key idea. A disc looks like a plane only while z is small compared with a. The bigger the disc, the higher P can rise before the field falls.
See itFinish the sweep on the 10 cm disc with P at 0.5 cm. Watch for: Height z of P reading 0.5 cm and Running Ez reading 5.37 × 10⁴ N/C, just under the 5.65 × 10⁴ N/C of the plane.

08

Far away, a disc is a point charge: Ez ≈ Q/4πε₀z²

For z ≫ a, expand the square root: z/√(a² + z²) = (1 + a²/z²)−1/2 ≈ 1 − a²/2z² (notes 1.20). The bracket becomes a²/2z², and

Q is the charge of the whole disc. From far away it looks like a point charge.

The 3 cm disc has Q = 2.83 nC. At z = 15 cm it gives 1.10 × 10³ N/C, 97 % of the point-charge value 1.13 × 10³ N/C. At z = 30 cm it gives 280 N/C, 99.3 % of 282 N/C. Doubling z from 15 to 30 cm leaves Ez at 0.256 of its value, close to a quarter.

The approximation improves with z/a: 97 % at z = 5a, 99.3 % at z = 10a. The 10 cm disc at 30 cm, only 3a, gives 92 %.

Key idea. Far from the disc only its total charge matters, and Ez falls as 1/z².
See itFinish the sweep on the 3 cm disc with P at 15 cm. Watch for: Disc charge Q reading 2.83 nC and Running Ez reading 1.10 × 10³ N/C.
See itNow raise P to 30 cm. Watch for: Running Ez falling to 280 N/C, about a quarter, with the graph label reading 280 N/C beside the point-charge value 282 N/C.
09

Summary

In one line. This sim adds up the fields of thin rings to build the field on the axis of a charged disc, for three disc radii and for an infinite plane.

Key points

  • A ring's field adds to Ez in proportion to its charge, its distance and its tilt together. Per centimetre of radius it peaks at s′ = z/√2.
  • Ez = (σ/2ε₀)(1 − cos θ), where θ is the rim angle at P. It depends on z and a only through z/a.
  • Close in, or for a plane, Ez = σ/2ε₀ = 5.65 × 10⁴ N/C. Far away, Ez ≈ Q/4πε₀z².

Common mix-ups

  • "The outer rings dominate, because they hold the most charge." They are also farther and more tilted. The contribution per centimetre peaks near 3.5 cm for z = 5 cm, at 4.35 × 10³ N/C per cm, against 2.02 × 10³ at the 10 cm rim.
  • "The field of a plane falls as you move away." It stays at 5.65 × 10⁴ N/C, because more of the plane comes into view.
  • "Doubling the distance quarters the field of any disc." That holds only far away. The 10 cm disc gives 5.37 × 10⁴ N/C at 0.5 cm and 5.09 × 10⁴ N/C at 1 cm.

Things to try on your own

  • Finish the 30 cm disc at z = 15 cm and compare with the 10 cm disc at z = 5 cm.
